greeting: Ask me anything about the AURAK Coding Club — what we run, how to join, or what Tech Titans is.
suggestions: Do I need to know how to code?

questions: what happens at a dev discussion
entries.answer:
Dev Discussions are our flagship activity — in-person deep dives into one computer science topic, held in G-201 and live streamed on Google Meet. Past sessions have covered cryptography, theory of computation, live-coding music in Sonic Pi, Unreal Engine, Vim and the internals of TeX.

A session runs about an hour and mixes a taught breakdown with a live project demo, an interactive Mentimeter quiz and often a typeathon. Bring a laptop. Turning up earns you a x4 multiplier on the Tech Titans leaderboard, and showcasing your own project earns x16.
citations: Dev Discussions — the club's flagship activity

questions: What actually happens in the hour?
what do you do in a dev discussion
entries.answer:
Each session opens with a short introduction, then spends most of the hour on a taught breakdown of the topic. After that there is usually a live demo — someone building or running the thing on screen — followed by a Mentimeter quiz that the room answers together, and often a typeathon to close.

The Vim session in October ran exactly this way: five minutes of introduction, thirty minutes of breakdown, fifteen on Mentimeter and ten on the typeathon.
citations: Dev Discussions — the club's flagship activity

entries.answer:
In G-201, the AutoCAD lab on the AURAK campus. That has been the home room for essentially every Dev Discussion we have run.

If you cannot make it in person, sessions are live streamed on Google Meet, so you can follow along from anywhere.
citations: Dev Discussions — the club's flagship activity

entries.answer:
Yes — every Dev Discussion is live streamed on Google Meet so members who cannot attend in person can still follow along. Sessions have been broadcast this way since early on.

Coming in person is better if you can, though. The Mentimeter quizzes and typeathons are a lot more fun in a room full of people, and bringing a laptop lets you follow along hands-on.
citations: Dev Discussions — the club's flagship activity

questions: Can beginners come to a Dev Discussion?
do i need to be good at coding to attend
entries.answer:
Absolutely. The sessions are pitched as introductions to a topic, not as lectures for people who already know it — the Vim session was billed as an introductory crash course, and the Sonic Pi one started from what a waveform is.

We are a club that welcomes complete beginners alongside experienced programmers, and nobody is going to test you at the door. Come along and see.
citations: Dev Discussions — the club's flagship activity

questions: Do I need to prepare anything?
do i need to read anything first
entries.answer:
Just bring a laptop if you have one — several sessions have been explicitly bring-your-own-device, and the hands-on parts are much better when you can follow along.

There is no reading to do beforehand. Each session is self-contained and starts from the basics of its topic.
citations: Dev Discussions — the club's flagship activity

entries.answer:
A wide range. Cryptography and applied number theory, regular languages and theory of computation, live-coding music with Sonic Pi alongside the Music Club, markup languages including Markdown, HTML and LaTeX, game development in Unreal Engine, a Vim crash course, and a session unpacking the low-level behaviour of TeX.

The common thread is extracurricular computer science — things you would not normally meet in a course.
citations: Dev Discussions — the club's flagship activity

questions: Tell me about the Vim session
entries.answer:
The Vim Crash Course ran on 23rd October 2025 in G-201, presented by Mohammed Alshamsi — known around here as the resident flying whale.

It covered modal editing, the navigation and motion grammar, the operator-plus-text-object grammar that makes Vim composable, and then went further into registers, macros, marks and batch commands. It closed with a Mentimeter round and a typeathon.
citations: Dev Discussions — the club's flagship activity

questions: Tell me about the cryptography session
entries.answer:
Our first Dev Discussion, on 14th March 2024 in G-201, presented by Mohammed Alshamsi. It went from divisibility and the Euclidean algorithm through primes, modular arithmetic and Euler's totient function, and used all of it to build up to real ciphers.

The session covered the Caesar and affine ciphers and then RSA itself, and the Mentimeter round had the room decrypting messages by hand.
citations: Dev Discussions — the club's flagship activity

questions: Tell me about the music session
entries.answer:
Experience the Sound of Code ran on 28th October 2024 with the Music Club — an introduction to Sonic Pi, the open-source live-coding music environment built on Ruby.

It covered synths, loops and conditionals, then built up to real pieces: a multi-threaded cover of He's a Pirate with reverb and a bit-crushed bassline, Twinkle Twinkle, and note sequences generated straight out of a sine function.

entries.answer:
Tech Titans is our semesterly leaderboard, set up to reward getting involved. Everyone starts on 1 point and climbs by activating multipliers — you enter the leaderboard the moment you earn your first one.

At the end of each semester the top three receive Coding Club Tech Titan certificates.

Everything multiplies rather than adds. Voting on a Tech Talk poll is x2. Attending a Dev Discussion, getting featured in the meme competition, volunteering, or shipping a major update to a project you already submitted are each x4. Winning a typeathon or a Mentimeter question, or taking part in an official competition, is x8.

The big ones are x16 for showcasing a project at a Dev Discussion, and x32 for placing in a competition or winning best project of the semester.

questions: Why are the scores so big?
how did someone get billions of points
entries.answer:
Because the multipliers compound rather than adding up, scores get out of hand very quickly — which is entirely the point of a binary-themed system.

Our Fall 2024 winner, Abdulghani Sabbagh, finished the semester on 590,295,810,358,705,651,712 points. That is a real number from a real leaderboard.

There are. Not meeting the responsibilities of a volunteer position halves your score, repeatedly ignoring club guidelines divides it by four, and plagiarism or cheating in a club competition divides it by eight.

In practice they almost never come up — but a leaderboard with no downside would not mean much.

questions: How do I start earning points?
how do i get on the leaderboard
how do i join tech titans
entries.answer:
Come to a Dev Discussion — that is a x4 multiplier and the easiest way onto the board. Voting on a Tech Talk poll is another easy x2.

Every member starts on 1 point by default, and you appear on the leaderboard as soon as you activate your first multiplier. There is nothing to sign up for beyond being a member.

Major Wars is the side competition that runs alongside the individual leaderboard — everyone's points are also totalled up by academic major.

Artificial Intelligence took it in Spring 2024, then Computer Engineering won both Summer and Fall 2024. It is a good-natured rivalry and a reason to drag your coursemates along.

questions: how can i become a member
entries.answer:
Come and talk to us at the stand — we can get you signed up on the spot, and someone will walk you through what is coming up this semester.

Membership is open to every AURAK student, from any major and any skill level. There is no application to pass and no experience required.

questions: Do I need to know how to code?
entries.answer:
Not at all. The club is explicitly for complete beginners as well as experienced programmers, and plenty of our members joined knowing nothing.

Our leaderboard has included students from Mass Communication, Business, Architecture, Biotechnology and several engineering disciplines — not just computing majors. If you are curious, you already qualify.

questions: Can I join if I am not a CS major?
im not a computer science student
is it only for cs students
entries.answer:
Yes. Members come from right across the university — Artificial Intelligence, Computer Science, Computer Engineering, Electrical, Mechanical, Civil and Chemical Engineering, Mass Communication, Biotechnology, Architecture and Business have all been represented on our leaderboard.

You do not have to be a computing major to join, and you will not be the only non-specialist in the room.

questions: how do i join the crew
can i help run the club
entries.answer:
The crew is the team that runs the club rather than only attending it — President, Vice President, Technical Lead, Event Manager, Executive, Social Media Manager, Graphic Designer and Photographer.

We are currently recruiting for Social Media Manager, Graphic Designer and Photographer/Videographer. If any of those sound like you, talk to a crew member at the stand.
citations: Joining the club, and getting in touch

questions: How much time does it take?
entries.answer:
As much or as little as you want. Dev Discussions are the main fixture and each is about an hour; plenty of members come to those and nothing else.

There is no attendance requirement and nothing you have to keep up with. The Tech Titans leaderboard rewards turning up, but never punishes you for not.
citations: Dev Discussions — the club's flagship activity

entries.answer:
There is nothing to pay to be a member — we are a student club, and everything we run is free to attend.

Come to a Dev Discussion, read the Tech Talk, take part in the leaderboard: none of it costs anything.
citations: Joining the club, and getting in touch

entries.answer:
Tech Talk is our weekly newsletter, published as a magazine — news, announcements, member projects, polls and programming memes, laid out like a newspaper front page.

Voting on its polls is worth a x2 multiplier on the leaderboard, and it is where we announce what is coming up.

questions: Can I write for Tech Talk?
entries.answer:
Yes — there is a recurring column called Peer2Peer that carries member writing, and we are always looking for pieces.

Write about any topic that inspires you, tech-related or otherwise, and email it to codingclub2024@aurak.ac.ae. Getting featured also puts you on the leaderboard.

Review Rounds are review videos we post to our YouTube channel to help AURAK students prepare for midterms and finals.

They were set up in Spring 2024 and we have posted them most semesters since — a straightforward way the club tries to be useful during exam season.

A timed typing contest. We usually run one at the end of a Dev Discussion — it takes about ten minutes and is a good way to close a session.

Winning one is worth a x8 multiplier on the Tech Titans leaderboard.

We do — official Coding Club competitions alongside the lighter typeathons and meme competitions.

Taking part is worth a x8 multiplier on the leaderboard, and placing first, second or third is worth x32. They are among the biggest scoring opportunities of the semester.

Yes. We organise visits to conferences and technology events off campus — most recently a trip to WETEX 2024, one of the largest technology exhibitions in the region.

They are a chance to see the industry side of things, meet people well beyond the university, and spend a day with other members outside a lab.

questions: Do you work with other clubs?
entries.answer:
Often. We have run joint events with the Gaming Club and the Volunteering Club on a Rubik's Cube event, with the Music Club on the Experience the Sound of Code session, and with the Book Club on Books & Bytes, a tech-themed summer reading list and discussion.

Cross-club events tend to be some of the most fun things we do.

Commends is our collection of recommended resources — books, courses, websites and tools — with a short write-up of each and commentary from members who have used them.

It covers programming, compilers, data structures and algorithms, mathematics, theory of computation and systems. Anyone can contribute by opening a pull request on our GitHub.

We are the student coding and technology club at the American University of Ras Al Khaimah — a community for anyone interested in code, from complete beginners to people who have been programming for years.

Our flagship activity is Dev Discussions, deep dives into a computer science topic held in G-201. Alongside that we publish the weekly Tech Talk newsletter, post Review Rounds exam-prep videos, and run competitions, typeathons and trips to tech events.
citations: Dev Discussions — the club's flagship activity

entries.answer:
We have won AURAK's Most Active Student Club Award twice — for Spring 2024 and again for Fall 2024.

That second one came off the back of a busy semester: the club fair, a trip to WETEX, the freshman orientation event, and collaborations with three other clubs.

The club is run by a student crew. Riyad Almasri is President and Ahmed Fadhl is Vice President, with Mukerem Shifa as Technical Lead, Hewan Gete as Event Manager and Hussain Para as Executive.

We are currently recruiting a Social Media Manager, a Graphic Designer and a Photographer/Videographer.

Email us at codingclub2024@aurak.ac.ae — that reaches the crew and is the best route for anything that needs a real answer.

You can also find all our work on GitHub at github.com/AURAK-Coding-Club, and of course you can just talk to whoever is at the stand.
citations: Joining the club, and getting in touch

entries.answer:
Everything we do is public at github.com/AURAK-Coding-Club — the Tech Talk issues, the Dev Discussions agendas and slides, the Commends resource collection, our slide-deck template, and a verifiable credentials system we built for issuing club certificates.

Contributions are welcome; several of those repositories take pull requests from members.

questions: How long has the club been around?
entries.answer:
The club has been running for several years, but Spring 2024 was when it was substantially rebuilt — new branding, a new management team, faculty sponsors, and the launch of Tech Talks, Dev Discussions and Review Rounds all in one semester.

That semester won us our first Most Active Student Club Award, and we won it again in Fall 2024.

We hold to respect, inclusivity, collaboration, professionalism, integrity, safety, diversity and responsibility — and we mean the first one in particular. Members are expected to treat each other well regardless of background, identity or skill level.

Anything that falls short of that is dealt with by the crew. We also follow AURAK's own rules and the cultural values of the UAE.
